# Dominated midpoint coupling and the conditional three-fiber theorem

This proves a conditional case, not the full mixed-integer conjecture. The
only condition on the candidate below is that the actual mixed-volume
centroid has integer base coordinate. There are exactly three consecutive
positive-volume fibers. No restriction is imposed on continuous dimension,
fiber shapes, or the orientation of a containing halfspace.

## 1. A dominated midpoint coupling

Let A,C be bounded measurable subsets of R^d of the same positive volume a.
There is a probability coupling pi of their uniform probability measures
such that the finite measure

    eta = a ((x,y)->(x+y)/2)#pi

is dominated by d-dimensional Lebesgue measure. Its mass is a and its
centroid is the average of the two ordinary centroids. If (A+C)/2 is
contained in a compact convex set B, then eta is supported in B and hence
eta <= 1_B dx. For every closed halfspace H in R^d,

    eta(H) <= |A intersect H|+|C intersect H|.           (1)

More generally, (1) applies to an affine functional with different affine
offsets at the two endpoints, provided its midpoint value is the average
of its two endpoint values.

Here is a direct construction, including the passage to nonsmooth sets.
First let f,g be smooth strictly positive probability densities on R^d,
both bounded above by 1/a, obtained by convolving bounded compactly supported
densities with a nondegenerate centered Gaussian. Construct a triangular
map T by matching successive conditional distribution functions. Namely,
T_1 matches the first-coordinate marginal CDFs, and, recursively, T_j
matches the conditional CDF of x_j given x_1,...,x_(j-1) to that of the
j-th target coordinate given T_1,...,T_(j-1). These conditional densities
are smooth and strictly positive. Their CDFs increase from zero to one.
The implicit function theorem and recursive inversion show that T is a
smooth triangular diffeomorphism with positive diagonal derivatives.
The Gaussian convolution justifies differentiation of every marginal and
conditional integral locally. Differentiating the conditional CDF equations
and multiplying their diagonal identities gives

    det DT(x) = f(x)/g(T(x)),

and change of variables gives T#(f dx)=g dx.

The map F=(Id+T)/2 is also a triangular diffeomorphism. With earlier
coordinates fixed, its j-th coordinate is strictly increasing and tends
to the two infinite endpoints, and its diagonal derivative is
(1+partial_j T_j)/2. The arithmetic-geometric mean inequality gives

    det DF(x) >= sqrt(det DT(x)).

Consequently the density of F#(f dx), evaluated at F(x), is

    f(x)/det DF(x) <= sqrt(f(x)g(T(x))) <= 1/a.          (2)

Apply this to f_epsilon=(1_A/a)*phi_epsilon and
g_epsilon=(1_C/a)*phi_epsilon, where phi_epsilon is the centered Gaussian
density with covariance epsilon^2 Id. Their upper bounds are 1/a. The
joint laws of (X,T_epsilon(X)) are tight, since both marginal families
converge weakly to compactly supported uniform laws. Extract a weakly
convergent subsequence. One can use ordinary tight-measure compactness;
equivalently restrict to growing compact boxes, extract on each box, and
diagonalize using the uniform bound on mass outside those boxes. The limit
pi has exactly the original uniform marginals on A,C, by weak convergence
of Gaussian convolution to the original measures. The application below
uses compact convex bodies.
The midpoint pushforwards converge weakly because the midpoint map is
continuous. For every nonnegative compactly supported continuous test
function, (2) gives integral eta_epsilon test <= integral test dx. Passing
to the limit proves eta<=dx. The coupling marginals give its centroid
directly; no interchange of unbounded moments is necessary at this step.
Its support lies in (A+C)/2 in the compact-set case. Finally the elementary
pointwise inequality

    1_H((x+y)/2) <= 1_H(x)+1_H(y)

proves (1), including all closed boundaries. The same argument proves the
stated affine-offset variant. This completes the construction needed below.

## 2. Conditional OC for three consecutive positive fibers

Let d>=1, and suppose the positive fibers of a convex body in R x R^d are
A,B,C at integer coordinates -1,0,1, with no other positive fibers. Suppose
its mixed-volume centroid has integer first coordinate. Since both endpoint
masses are positive, the centroid's first coordinate is strictly between
-1 and 1, so it is zero. Hence |A|=|C|=a. Write |B|=b. Convexity implies
(A+C)/2 subset B, and ordinary Brunn-Minkowski implies b>=a.

Use Section 1 to obtain eta<=1_B dx with mass a and centroid
(g_A+g_C)/2. Put rho=1_B dx+2eta. Its mass is b+2a, and its centroid is

    g=(b g_B+a g_A+a g_C)/(b+2a),

exactly the continuous coordinate of the actual mixed-volume centroid.
In particular (0,g) is a single point of the middle fiber.

The bounded-density centroid inequality proved in
`candidate d4ddcd5e9c4567f8` states that every continuous
closed halfspace Q containing g satisfies

    |B intersect Q|+eta(Q) >= gamma_d (b+2a)/2.          (3)

Now let H be ANY closed ambient halfspace containing (0,g), with its
affine margin L(z,x)>=0. For every coupled pair (x,y),

    L(0,(x+y)/2)=[L(-1,x)+L(1,y)]/2.

The offset version of (1) therefore gives

    eta(H_0) <= |A intersect H_-1|+|C intersect H_1|.

If H_0 is a proper continuous halfspace, combine this with (3). If H_0
is all of R^d, the same conclusion follows from b+a>=gamma_d(b+2a)/2;
indeed the latter is immediate from gamma_d<=1 and b>=0. In both cases,

    vol_MI(S intersect H) >= gamma_d vol_MI(S)/2.

There is no empty central halfspace since (0,g) belongs to H. This includes
purely integer normals, oblique normals, and closed boundaries. Additional
zero-volume fibers do not change the centroid or any measured inequality.

The proof requires the integer-base centroid condition. For unequal
endpoint volumes that condition fails, and no rounding or replacement of
the candidate is implicit here. The general three-fiber statement and the
full theorem remain separate obligations.
